title: 8 kt chop: over-sheeted, set twist
brief: The leech is hooked and the top batten is inside the boom centreline, so the rig is stalled and the bow is stopping in every wave. Find the twist that keeps the boat moving through the chop.
hint: Twist buys acceleration out of the waves. Ease the sheet first, then carry the boom back up with the car.

title: 6 kt flat: too much backstay
brief: In six knots on flat water the mast is bent enough to flatten the main to nothing and the headstay is too straight for the jib entry. Power the rig back up.
hint: Light air wants depth and headstay sag. Backstay off until the mainsail shows draft again, then set the leech with the sheet.

title: 14 kt flat: depower without losing height
brief: Fourteen knots on flat water is a pointing mode, but this setup is fully powered and the boat is heeled past 22 degrees. Take power out of the top of the rig while keeping the leech loaded enough to hold a lane.
hint: Depower from the top down: backstay, then cunningham to pull the draft forward, then drop the car before you start easing sheet.

title: 10 kt: jib lead too far aft
brief: The jib lead is parked at the back of the track, so the foot is tight, the leech is open and the slot is dumping. The main is fine; the headsail is giving away height.
hint: Move the car forward until the upper leech stops falling away, then trim the sheet back on to close the slot.

title: 16 kt chop: vang and outhaul
brief: Sixteen knots and a short chop with the vang off and a deep foot: the boom is skying, the lower leech is unloaded and the boat is heeling instead of driving. Set the lower main.
hint: Vang holds the boom down so the traveller can work; outhaul flattens the bottom third. Backstay covers what is left up high.

title: 18 kt: everything on, keep the bow down
brief: Top of the range upwind. This setup is trimmed for 12 knots and the boat is pinned on its ear with the rudder loaded. Depower everything and find the mode that keeps the bow driving rather than climbing.
hint: Everything on, car down, and the main eased to the point where the top telltale streams half the time. Heel angle is the control variable, not the sheet load.

title: 12 kt: halyards and draft position
brief: Both halyards are soft and the cunningham has been used to compensate, so the draft sits aft in the main and there is a scallop up the jib luff. Fix the luff tension before the leech shape.
hint: Halyard sets the luff, cunningham trims the draft. Take the wrinkles out with halyard and the cunningham has almost nothing left to do at this wind speed.

title: 9 kt: inhauler and pointing
brief: Nine knots, smooth water, and the jib is sheeted wide with no inhaul, so the boat is fast and low in a fleet where height pays. Bring the clew inboard without choking the slot.
hint: Inhaul narrows the sheeting angle; the lead then has to come forward or the leech opens as you pull the clew in.

title: 10 kt: 140 or 150 degrees?
brief: Ten knots under the gennaker, sitting between the soak and the reaching mode. Set the kite for the angle you are actually sailing and see which side of the corner the VMG falls on.
hint: Tack line down projects the luff to windward for the low mode; ease it and trim on to reach. The luff should curl and be trimmed back continuously.

title: 20 kt: survival upwind
brief: Twenty knots and the boat is over-heeled with the traveller above centre. Nothing subtle is required: get the rig flat and the boat on its feet.
hint: Maximum backstay, car well below centre, and sheet to heel angle. Speed comes back the moment the boat stands up.
